items.content_html:
Perhaps one of the biggest pain point when calling the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Generative AI service (OCI GenAI) is authentication. Like all OCI REST APIs, request signing using an OCI API key is required to call the endpoints. That changed on January 21, 2026, when Oracle announced that developers can now generate "API Keys" that behave like most do with other LLM providers.

Create the API Keys​

  1. In the OCI Console, click on the navigation menu, and navigate to Analytics & AI > Generative AI.
  2. On the Generative AI service page, click on the new link to API Keys.
  3. Click on the button Create API key.
  4. Enter a name and description. Also, select the compartment to place the new API key.
  5. Scroll down, enter the names and expiry dates for both keys that will be generated, and then click the button Create.
  6. IMPORTANT Copy and store both generated keys safely. Then, click the button Close.
  7. If necessary, the keys can be regenerated from the API Key's details page.

IAM Policy​

The use of the API keys require an OCI Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy addition. Create or use an existing IAM policy, and add the following statement:

Allow any-user to use generative-ai-family in compartment <compartment_name> where ALL {request.principal.type='generativeaiapikey'}

Use the Keys​

Next, let's test the newly generated API keys.

NOTE

The commands below assume that you have access to Bash and curl and jq are installed.

  • Read the API key into a Bash environment variable. 
    # Prompt for either of the API keys.
    read -s API_KEY
  • Use curl to call the completions endpoint. The example below generates a simple text response. 
    curl --location 'https://inference.generativeai.us-chicago-1.oci.oraclecloud.com/20231130/actions/v1/chat/completions' \
        --header "Authorization: Bearer ${API_KEY}" \
        --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
        --silent \
        --data '{ "model": "xai.grok-4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "Where is the capital of Malaysia?" }]}' \
        | jq -r '.choices[0].message.content'
  • If the model used also supports multimedia inputs, set the IMAGE_URL. 
    IMAGE_URL="https://fuzziebrain.com/assets/images/sunrise-whitehorse-1280x720-c751de502eb414ff30940c710ca94c4e.jpg"
    Or, if you have an image on your file system, encode it using Base64: 
    IMAGE_URL="data:image/jpeg;base64,$(base64 -i samples/bird.jpg)"
  • Then, have the model generate a description of the image provided. 
    curl --location 'https://inference.generativeai.us-chicago-1.oci.oraclecloud.com/20231130/actions/v1/chat/completions' \
        --header "Authorization: Bearer ${API_KEY}" \
        --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
        --silent \
        --data '{ "model": "xai.grok-4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": [{"type":"text", "text": "What is in this image?"}, {"type":"image_url", "image_url": {"url": "'$IMAGE_URL'"}}]}]}' \
        | jq -r '.choices[0].message.content'

It is important to note that the completions endpoint is different from the URL used when calling OCI GenAI using the OCI REST APIs. There is an additional path /completions at the end of the URL. Also, when working with the endpoint, you should probably use OpenAI's documentation for API usage instructions.

Caveat​

Not all models are compatible the OCI OpenAI chat completions API. Currently, the supported models are:

  • Meta Llama
  • xAI Grok; and
  • OpenAI gpt-oss

As of this blog post, availability is also limited to the following regions:

  • Germany Central (Frankfurt)
  • India South (Hyderabad)
  • Japan Central (Osaka)
  • US East (Ashburn)
  • US Midwest (Chicago)
  • US West (Phoenix)

Closing Thoughts​

I am glad that Oracle is doing a lot to make more and more of its OCI services and offerings compatible with its competitors, thereby helping increase developer adoption!

items.content_html:
There were several product announcements and launches at the Oracle AI World 2025 held in Las Vegas last year. One particular product that caught my attention is the Oracle Private Agent Factory (OPAF) that Sandesh Rao spoke about extensively at the conference. The OPAF is designed to cut through the complexity of building enterprise-grade assistants. It’s essentially a no-code/low-code playground that allows both business users and engineers to rapidly design, test, and deploy intelligent "Private Agents" that can securely interact with enterprise data. Rather than getting bogged down in writing custom "glue code" to connect models to databases, the Agent Factory provides a visual environment to "wire" these components together into functional, context-aware workflows.

Here is a closer look at the features and capabilities that, I feel, make OPAF a significant move for enterprise AI:

  • The Template Gallery: To help teams get off the starting blocks even faster, the platform includes a Template Gallery. This is a curated collection of pre-configured agent flows and patterns that you can use as a foundation for your own projects, ensuring you don't have to start with a blank canvas when building common AI use cases. I used this quite a bit to understand how to get started building my own flows.
  • Pre-built Agents: The platform ships with specialized, pre-built agents designed to handle specific data tasks right out of the box:
    • Knowledge Agent: Your go-to for RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) over enterprise documents, using vector search to provide grounded, traceable answers from approved sources like SharePoint or Object Storage.
    • Data Analysis Agent: A powerhouse for structured data that doesn't just run SQL; it performs analysis to understand your tables and views, automatically generating visualizations and natural-language explanations. I briefly played with this one, and it reminded me of the cool Oracle Analytics Cloud feature called Auto Insights.
  • User Management: Security is baked in with robust user management that supports Single Sign-On (SSO) (think OAuth). This allows organizations to manage access centrally through existing corporate identity providers, ensuring that only authorized users can build or interact with private agents while maintaining a seamless login experience.
  • The No-Code Agent Builder: At the heart of the platform is a visual, drag-and-drop interface. It abstracts away the heavy lifting, letting you connect chat inputs, LLMs, and data sources, including native integration with the Oracle Autonomous AI Database using simple visual building blocks.
  • The Private AI Services Container: For those obsessed with data sovereignty, this is a "killer feature." OPAF works with privately hosted instances of LLMs, for example, Ollama and vLLM. This ensures your sensitive data never has to leave your controlled perimeter to visit a third-party AI provider.

Getting Started... Quick​

OPAF is available as a download through Oracle's Software Delivery Cloud. However, you can also find a click-to-launch application from the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Marketplace. Harry Snart covers this approach (and more) in detail on his blog post.

Deploying from the marketplace is a faster way to get started, however, I opted to deploy it "manually" on a compute for a few reasons:

  1. I typically use Network Security Groups (NSGs) to filter network traffic. The installation process after the compute and software are deployed will fail as it will have no egress rule to allow the required network communications.
  2. The OCI Stack creates the instance on a public subnet. I generally do not like to put a compute running web applications on a public subnet.
  3. The default OCI Compute shape selected is VM.Standard2.8. You can size it smaller, but if you changed the architecture to a "flex" shape like VM.Standard.E5.Flex, it doesn't allow you to assign fewer than 8 OCPUs and 64 GB memory, and it also comes with a 500 GB boot volume to start. That's probably an overkill for my first time.

Compute Setup and Installation​

As you work through the interactive installation process later, you will note that it has a option to execute commands on a Compute instantiated with an Oracle Enterprise Linux 8 (OEL8) image, and uses the user opc.

Network Security​

I typically use Network Security Groups when managing port access to OCI resources. For OPAF, ensure that there ingress rules for TCP ports 22 (SSH), and 8080 (OPAF web user inteface). If a quick start configuration is performed later, an instance of the Oracle AI Database 23c Free is deployed. Optionally, allow access to TCP port 1521 if you wish to connect to the database. Finally, ensure that there are egress rules to any OCI resources, e.g., Oracle Autonomous AI Database (ADB), and the Internet. If a proxy is not used, make sure that the compute routes to either an OCI Internet Gateway or NAT Gateway.

Resize Storage​

When creating the Compute instance, a custom boot volume was used.

Prerequisite Software​

There isn't any that the installer script will take care of.

Oracle Container Registry​

The Oracle Container Registry (OCR) is Oracle public repository of Docker containers for anyone to run their products as a container. It requires an Oracle account to login, and with the migration to SSO, an Auth Token is now required where a three-legged authentication cannot be performed. One example is the OPAF deployment process that we are about to embark on. If you haven't already done so, go to the OCR, and sign in with your Oracle account. Then follow these steps:

  1. Click your username on the top-right of the website to expose the options, and select the option Auth Token.
  2. Click the Generate Secret Key button.
  3. After the auth token has been created, click the Copy Secret Key link.

Download the Files​

Either download the software and then upload to the server's /tmp directory, or use Wget to download directly onto the server.

  1. On the OPAF download page on the Software Delivery Cloud, first select the appropriate platform. For example, Linux x86-64.
  2. Check to accept the license agreement.
  3. Click WGET Options.

Configure OPAF​

At the end of the installation process, a link would have been provide to get to OPAF's web frontend. I'm not sure about the choice of the port number 8080 for SSL/TLS access, but pay attention to use the HTTPS protocol when you access the URL via a browser. Also, the certificate is self-signed, so you can confidently ignore the error the first time you access OPAF.

Upon first use, the instance's base configuration must be performed.

  1. Begin by creating the administrator account by providing your email address and desired password, then click the Next button.
  2. Click the Install button to install the OPAF components.
  3. If the installation is successful, the button Next will be enabled. Click it to proceed to the LLM configuration step.
  4. OPAF requires a generative and embedding models to be configured. For generative models, four different LLM providers can be configured: OCI Generative AI (OCI GenAI), OpenAI, or locally using vLLM or Ollama. In the diagram below, I have configured it for OCI GenAI. The model ID, endpoint, compartment OCID, and OCI API key (plus user information) must be supplied.
  5. Configure the embedded with a local model, and click both Test connection buttons to ensure the instance can talk to the LLMs successfully.
  6. Save the generative and embedded model configurations, then click the Finish Installation button to complete the process.

Validate the Installation​

  1. Navigate to the same URL to OPAF, and login using the administrator credentials.
  2. After a successful login, navigate to the Prompt lab.
  3. Click to load one of the saved tests, choose a LLM, and click the Generate button to generate a response from the selected LLM.

Woohoo! My own private factory to generate all the agents I need to conquer the world! 😈

What's Next?​

items.content_html:
It seems that the rage about Model Context Protocol is continuing into the new year with Oracle announcing the release of the MCP server for Oracle Autonomous AI Database (ADB) in December, 2025. MCP's been around, but until now, I have yet to find a purpose beyond using a tool like Claude Desktop or Cline in Microsoft Visual Studio Code (Cline) to "talk" to my database. Hence, I made it a point to understand how we can work with MCP endpoints with code, and so, here's what I've learned in that journey.

Turning On the Taps​

The first thing that you'll need to do is to turn on the MCP server feature for your ADB. Unlike many of the other features like Oracle APEX, Oracle Machine Learning user interface, etc., the way to turn the MCP server feature on is to add a specific, free-form tag to the resource. Read this if you don't already know what resource tags are.

The name of this tag must be: adb$feature, and the value is this JSON:

{ "name": "mcp_server", "enable": true }

The elements should be self-explantory. Once added, the ADB will begin to update itself. If successful, the ADB's status should be in an Available state, and the tag is committed successfully. If not, and receive the error message below, then chances are, the MCP server feature is not yet available in your ADB's OCI region.

Error returned by Unknown operation operation in Unknown service service.(400, ADB-10000, false) The Autonomous AI Database operation failed due to an unknown error. Timestamp: 2025-12-24T17:19:54.775Z Client version: Oracle-JavaSDK/2.77.0 Request Endpoint: Unknown request endpoint Troubleshooting Tips: See https://docs.oracle.com/en-us/iaas/Content/API/References/apierrors.htm#apierrors_400__400_adb-10000 for more information about resolving this error Also see Unknown API reference link for details on this operation's requirements. To get more info on the failing request, you can enable debug level logs as mentioned in `Using SLF4J for Logging section` in https://docs.oracle.com/en-us/iaas/Content/API/SDKDocs/javasdkconfig.htm. If you are unable to resolve this Unknown service issue, please contact Oracle support and provide them this full error message

Follow the full set of instructions here to complete all the needed steps to enable the ADB MCP server. There are also instructions on how to configure MCP servers for Claude Desktop and Cline.

There are several components to an application that supports MCP. First, it requires a MCP server, in this case, that's the ADB. Then, we need a MCP client that connects to the server. The application then acts as the MCP host that uses these MCP clients to achieve its goals. As of today, MCP supports only two transport methods for communications between the clients and servers: Stdio and Streamable HTTP. Stdio, or standard input and output, is a local stream between the client and server. A server that only supports Stdio will need to be running on the same host as the client. The Streamable HTTP, on the other hand, allows communications between client and server using HTTP with Server-Sent Events. As communications are sent over the HTTP protocol, servers can also implement standard authentication protocol like bearer tokens, APIs, and OAuth.

Since the ADB is a managed service, one might naturally expect that it supports the second transport mechanism. This presents a little challenge to use within the database environment. To secure the MCP server, the service supports either OAuth or bearer token authentication. In the example later, I opt to use bearer tokens.

Tools for AI Agents​

The ADB's MCP server feature exposes custom tools that have been created in the database. These tools are created using the Select AI Agents PL/SQL procedure DBMS_CLOUD_AI_AGENT.CREATE_TOOL, and the access In my previous [blog post](/content/build-autonomous-apex-applications-joelkallmanday, I had created some tools including the INVENTORY_SEARCH_TOOL for searching the FLEET_PART table, and that is what I will use to run the example here. For your convenience, here's a summary of the code:

/**
 * Create the AI profile for searching the FLEET_PART table using natural
 * language.
 */
begin
  begin
    dbms_cloud_ai.drop_profile(
      profile_name => '&ai_profile_name._for_inventory'
    );
  exception
    when others then null;
  end;

  dbms_cloud_ai.create_profile(
    profile_name => '&ai_profile_name._for_inventory',
    attributes => '{
          "provider": "oci",
          "credential_name": "OCI_CRED",
          "object_list": [{"owner": "demo02", "name": "FLEET_PART"}],
          "comments": true,
          "annotations": true
      }'
    , description => 'AI profile for searching the fleet part table'
  );
end;

/**
 * Create the tool for AI agent to use to search the FLEET_PART table when it
 * rationalizes that it needs it.
 */
declare
  c_tool_name constant varchar2(128) := 'inventory_search_tool';
begin
  begin
    dbms_cloud_ai_agent.drop_tool(
      tool_name => c_tool_name
    );
  exception
    when others then null;
  end;

  dbms_cloud_ai_agent.create_tool(
    tool_name => c_tool_name
    , attributes => json_object(
      'tool_type' value 'SQL'
        , 'tool_params' value json_object(
          'profile_name' value '&ai_profile_name._for_inventory'
        )
    )
    , description => trim(q'[
This tool is used for searching the fleet part inventory. It should be used to
lookup fleet parts using either the part number or description.
    ]')
  );
end;

Note that the schema used to create the tool must have the necessary database privileges not only to create the tool, but to perform the task, such as accessing the data. For simplicity, I am connecting to the MCP server using the same database user that both created the tool and contains the table to be queried.

Discovering and Using the Tool​

To help understand how I can use remote MCP servers with code, I started with the Python SDK from OpenRouter, and thus the code is based on what they've provided in the tutorial. Then, since I have access to the OCI Generative AI (OciGenAi) service, I swapped out the LLM calls using the OCI OpenAI compatible SDK

These days, I work on Python projects using uv. You'll want that installed locally if you'd like to follow along. Then execute the following commands:

uv init adb-mcp-client
cd adb-mcp-client
uv add mcp python-dotenv requests oci-genai

My final pyproject.toml looks like this:

[project]
name = "adb-mcp-client"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.13"
dependencies = [
    "mcp>=1.25.0",
    "oci-openai>=1.0.0",
    "python-dotenv>=1.2.1",
    "requests>=2.32.5",
]

The code starts with the following import statements:

import asyncio, os, requests, httpx, json, logging

from typing import Optional
from contextlib import AsyncExitStack

from mcp import ClientSession
from mcp.client.streamable_http import streamable_http_client
from oci_openai import AsyncOciOpenAI, OciUserPrincipalAuth
from dotenv import load_dotenv

The python-dotenv package is used then used to load and set more sensitive or dynamic variables. Add a file .env with the variables below, setting their values according to your environment.

ADB_OCID="ocid1.autonomousdatabase.oc1.phx..."
REGION_ID="us-phoenix-1"
DB_USER="mydbuser"
DB_PASSWORD="mysecretpasswordincleartext"
PROFILE_NAME="my-oci-profile-name"
SERVICE_ENDPOINT="https://inference.generativeai.us-chicago-1.oci.oraclecloud.com"
COMPARTMENT_ID="ocid1.compartment.oc1.."

Load and set the variables from the .env file by calling the function load_dotenv(). The URLs for authenticating and communicating with the MCP servers, DATABASE_AUTH_URL and DATABASE_URL, are constructed using these variables. The user prompt to be sent to the LLM is also set in the variable QUESTION.

load_dotenv()

REGION_ID = os.getenv("REGION_ID")
ADB_OCID = os.getenv("ADB_OCID")
DB_USER = os.getenv("DB_USER")
DB_PASSWORD = os.getenv("DB_PASSWORD")
DATABASE_URL = f"https://dataaccess.adb.{REGION_ID}.oraclecloudapps.com/adb/mcp/v1/databases/{ADB_OCID}"
DATABASE_AUTH_URL = f"https://dataaccess.adb.{REGION_ID}.oraclecloudapps.com/adb/auth/v1/databases/{ADB_OCID}/token"

PROFILE_NAME = os.getenv("PROFILE_NAME")
SERVICE_ENDPOINT = os.getenv("SERVICE_ENDPOINT")
COMPARTMENT_ID = os.getenv("COMPARTMENT_ID")
MODEL_NAME = "openai.gpt-oss-120b"

QUESTION = "My 2010 Toyota Prius aircon is emitting a foul smell. Do you have a replacement filter?"

Next, authenticate to the ADB's MCP server using a database account.

auth_response = requests.post(
    url=DATABASE_AUTH_URL,
    headers={
        "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded",
        "Accept": "application/json"
    },
    data={
        "grant_type": "password",
        "username": DB_USER,
        "password": DB_PASSWORD
    }
)

NOTE: that the official documentation says to send the content-type header with the value application/json, but that didn't work for me, and thus switched to application/x-www-form-urlencoded.

The response will have a HTTP status code 200 if authentication is successful. The code below demonstrates how we would proceed to:

  1. Obtain a bearer token for the database user to be used to communicate with the MCP server.
  2. Create a httpx client with the authorization header set with the bearer token received. Note that interactions with the MCP server might take a while, and the default timeout for the httpx client may be insufficient. Set it to a reasonable value.
  3. Create a MCP client session.
  4. Obtain a list of tools available to the database user through the MCP server.
  5. Initialize a LLM client, in this case, using the OCI OpenAI compatible SDK.
  6. Start building the message stream, beginning with the system prompt, and the user's query specified in the variable QUESTION.
  7. Call the chat completion endpoint, supplying the messages and list of available tools from the MCP server.
  8. Extend the messages chain with the response.
  9. Check the response to see if a tool call is required.
  10. If tool calling is requested, extract the name and arguments, then use the MCP client to make the requested tool call.
  11. If the tool called responds successfully, append the results to the message chain.
  12. Make a second and final call to the LLM to generate the response for the user, and display it.
if auth_response.status_code == 200:
    bearer_token = auth_response.json().get("access_token") #1

    async with httpx.AsyncClient( #2
      headers={ "Authorization": f"Bearer {bearer_token}"},
      timeout=300
    ) as client:
        async with streamable_http_client(
          url=DATABASE_URL,
          http_client=client
        ) as (read, write, _):
            async with ClientSession(read, write) as session: #3
                final_response = None
                await session.initialize()
                tools = await session.list_tools() #4
                available_tools = [convert_tool_format(tool) for tool in tools.tools]

                async with AsyncOciOpenAI( #5
                    service_endpoint=SERVICE_ENDPOINT,
                    auth=OciUserPrincipalAuth(profile_name=PROFILE_NAME),
                    compartment_id=COMPARTMENT_ID
                ) as llm:
                    messages=[ #6
                        {
                            "role": "system",
                            "content": "You are an experienced car mechanic. Use only the tools available to you to answer the question. Do NOT hallucinate."
                        }
                    ]

                    messages.append(
                        {
                            "role": "user",
                            "content": QUESTION
                        }
                    )

                    response = await llm.chat.completions.create( #7
                        model=MODEL_NAME,
                        tools=available_tools,
                        messages=messages
                    )

                    content = response.choices[0].message
                    messages.append(content.model_dump()) #8

                    if content.tool_calls is not None: #9
                        tool_name = content.tool_calls[0].function.name #10
                        tool_args = content.tool_calls[0].function.arguments #10
                        tool_args = json.loads(tool_args) if tool_args else {} #10

                        try:
                            result = await session.call_tool(tool_name, tool_args) #10
                        except Exception as e:
                            logging.error(f"Error calling tool {tool_name}: {e}")
                            result = None

                        messages.append({ #11
                            "role": "tool",
                            "tool_call_id": content.tool_calls[0].id,
                            "name": tool_name,
                            "content": str(result.content[0])
                        })

                        response = await llm.chat.completions.create( #12
                            model=MODEL_NAME,
                            messages=messages
                        )

                        final_response = f"Your question was:\n{QUESTION}\n\nMy response:\n{response.choices[0].message.content}" #12
                    else:
                        final_response = content.content

                    print(final_response) #12

NOTE: The MCP tool definitions do not quite work with the OpenAI interface, so thanks OpenRouter, I had to include a helper function shared in their instructions.

def convert_tool_format(self, tool):
    converted_tool = {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": tool.name,
            "description": tool.description,
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": tool.inputSchema["properties"],
                "required": tool.inputSchema["required"]
            }
        }
    }

    return converted_tool

When running in "debug mode", we can see how the first LLM call results in the determination that tool calling is required, and it is specific to what has been exposed by the MCP server.

Do you have a replacement filter?'}, {'content': None, 'refusal': None, 'role': 'assistant', 'annotations': None, 'audio': None, 'function_call': None, 'tool_calls': [{'id': 'call_20559012-b312-4547-9210-8b32e4e0e743', 'function': {'arguments': '{\n  "ACTION": "RUNSQL",\n  "QUERY": "Find cabin air filter for 2010 Toyota Prius in inventory"\n}', 'name': 'INVENTORY_SEARCH_TOOL'}, 'type': 'function'}], 'reasoning_content': "User asks about replacement filter for a 2010 Toyota Prius aircon emitting foul smell. As a car mechanic, we need to determine if we have a replacement filter, likely the cabin air filter. We can search inventory for a cabin air filter for 2010 Toyota Prius. Use INVENTORY_SEARCH_TOOL with ACTION RUNSQL maybe. The tool can query. Let's do that."}]

Specifically, in the log message below, we see that the tool to call involves the Select AI's RUNSQL operation, with the query in natural language.

When the tool is invoked by the code, the ADB then queries and return the results using its natural language to SQL (NL2SQL) capabilities, i.e., it takes the query text generated by the LLM, generates an appropriate SQL query, executes the query, then returns the results. The results of the tool invocation are shown below.

Your question was:

My response:
The unpleasant odor coming from the air‑conditioning system is most often caused by a **dirty or clogged cabin‑air filter**. When the filter gets saturated with pollen, dust, mold spores or other contaminants it can circulate a musty, “wet‑dog” smell every time the HVAC blows.

items.content_html:
Almost a year ago, I wrote about the OCI Generative AI Agents service that can be used to create a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) application using the service. I'm glad to see that the offering has since expanded, and also available in more regions. You can now easily create AI agents that have access to not just the RAG tool, but SQL, function, and other agents, no coding required! However, we are still limited to using the Llama model that is preselected by the service, and may be a problem with customers who are not able to agree to the terms and conditions of use, due to country-specific laws.

Fortunately, there's a solution. Read on.

What is an AI Agent?​

The term "AI Agent" is everywhere now, usually referring to a system powered by a Large Language Model (LLM) that can autonomously plan, break down a goal, use tools (like a search engine or code interpreter), and execute steps to get things done. This is a massive leap in what we consider "autonomy" in software. But here’s the thing: the core idea of an intelligent, goal-directed agent isn't new; it's the result of decades of foundational research.

The earliest, most traditional form of this concept was the Intelligent Agent, and if you've been following my writings and presentations, this was my favourite subject when I was work on my graduate degree at the Institute of System Science, National University of Singapore. Below is a snippet of a term paper I wrote on the automatic bartering of computing resources using intelligent agents.

In classical AI, this was an abstract entity formally defined by its ability to perceive its environment and act rationally to achieve its design goals. This was the era of Symbolic AI, where intelligence was defined by clear, explicit logic.

A perfect example of this is JADE (Java Agent DEvelopment Framework). JADE is an open-source platform that was instrumental in building Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), where multiple agents collaborate. JADE provided the standardized "plumbing" (like the Agent Communication Language, or ACL) so developers could focus on an agent's logic. An agent built with JADE knew things because a human expert hand-coded those things as formal rules or explicit knowledge graphs.

Today, LLMs have largely superseded the need for traditional symbolic knowledge systems in agent design. We no longer rely on human experts or consortiums to meticulously handwrite logic rules and formal knowledge bases (the old Symbolic AI approach). Instead, the agents' reasoning and internal "rules" are learned implicitly by training massive artificial neural networks on vast amounts of data, creating highly flexible and general-purpose intelligence.

My preparations for Kscope25 led me down a technical rabbit hole. I wasn't satisfied with using pre-built frameworks; I needed to understand the native mechanics of modern AI Agents. My goal was to implement an agent from scratch. I sourced a foundational Python example that walks through the entire process: defining the agent's reasoning chain, enabling it to select and execute tools, and managing the core decision-making loop. That's where I learned that the basic outline of what AI Agents do is this:

  1. Load all the required environment variables like API keys.
  2. Configure a LLM client for use by the agent.
  3. Define the tools. In the example, there were two:
    1. wikipedia(q): Queries the Wikipedia API for a search term and returns the plain text summary snippet.
    2. calculate(operation): Uses Python's eval() to securely calculate a mathematical expression (e.g., "5.972e24 * 2").
  4. Define an "Agent" class that stores the LLM client and maintains a history of the conversation, prepopulated with a system prompt. The system prompt defines the core ReAct Loop structure: Thought → Action → PAUSE → Observation → (Loop), and provides the LLM with the syntax for using the available tools (wikipedia and calculate), and a few examples (few-shot training) of how to respond to a user prompt.
  5. Instantiate the Agent class, providing it with the LLM client to use, and a list of tools that it has access to.
  6. When a user prompt is received, loop until either an "answer" can be determined, or the maximum number of iterations is reached.
  7. In each iteration:
    1. Generate response by sending the next_prompt (either the initial query or a new Observation) to the LLM via agent(next_prompt). The LLM's response is stored in result.
    2. Look for a final answer. If result contains the keyword "Answer", the agent has completed the task and the loop terminates.
    3. If an answer is not found, then look for an "action" request, for example, if result contains "PAUSE" and the format "Action: tool_name: argument". If tool use is required, then:
      1. Determine what tool to use.
      2. Execute the tool and capture its results.
      3. Prepare the next prompt. It should have an "observation" that includes the results from executing the tool.
      4. Continue to the next iteration the new "observation" prompt. This allows the agent to use the information in its next "thought".
    4. Append each response (the LLM's thought, action, or answer) to the conversation history.

NOTE

If a tool is not found or there's an error in the result, then the next prompt is set to an error message, which the LLM then sees and adapts to in the next iteration.

I hope that gently explains what a basic AI agent does to provide you intelligent and contextual response. And if it helps, here's a recent quote that I came across that quite recently.

An LLM agent runs tools in a loop to achieve a goal. ~ Simon Willison

You can read his full blog post here.

I would also add that a good agent also has good prompts and carefully crafted examples (for "learning"), and thus, it's mostly what Simon said but also a little bit of prompt engineering skills is required. A good place to start is by using well-published prompts to get start. One great example is the ReAct prompt by Harrison Chase.

Agentic AI Frameworks​

There are quite a few good agentic AI frameworks that you can use today if you live in the Python world, just so you don't need to code everything from scratch. Great examples include:

  • CrewAI (LangChain based)
  • AutoGen
  • LangGraph (also uses LangChain)
  • LlamaIndex
  • Smolgents

Writing a AI agent using Smolagents could be as simple as this!

import os

from smolagents import CodeAgent, WebSearchTool, LiteLLMModel
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()

GROQ_API_KEY = os.environ["GROQ_API_KEY"]

def main():
    model = LiteLLMModel(
        model_id="groq/gemma2-9b-it",
        api_key=GROQ_API_KEY,
    )
    agent = CodeAgent(tools=[WebSearchTool()], model=model, stream_outputs=True)

    agent.run("How many seconds will it take for a car to travel 500 metres if \
        the driver drives at the speed limit on Hwy 1 in Vancouver?")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Here's the code in action.

That's great! But what about Oracle? Are there any great agentic AI tools that we can use? Of course there is!

OCI Select AI Agents​

For starters, I mentioned the OCI Generative AI Agents service that allows you to create and define AI agents without any code. As mentioned in the opening paragraph, there have been several additions to the service since my previous post. Beyond knowledge bases, or RAG tooling, developers now have access to function calling, executing SQL queries on private Oracle Databases, and interacting with other agents.

The service allows you to define custom endpoints that may or may not include sessions (think conversational histories), guardrails, and more. Each endpoint is available as a REST API call. I will not going into details on how to work with this endpoint as I had already done so in the previous article.

At the time of writing, this service is currently available in the following regions:

  • US Midwest (Chicago)
  • Germany Central (Frankfurt)
  • UK South(London)
  • Brazil East (Sao Paulo)
  • Japan Central (Osaka)
  • US East (Ashburn)
  • US West (Phoenix)

However, as I eluded to at the start of this blog post, at this time, it is not possible to select a specific LLM. Today, the service uses Meta's Llama 3 model, and there are specific usage agreements that users have to agree to. I'm no legal expert but it does primarily affect folks in the European Union where privacy laws are stricter. If that's not you then this is an easy way to get started.

Select AI Agent​

Select AI Agent is an extension of Select AI that was recently announced through the October release notes for the Oracle Autonomous Database (ADB).

With this new capability, developers can create agentic workflows using only SQL and PL/SQL that support AI-driven automation, data interaction, and maintain human-in-the-loop control. These agents can plan and perform actions using built-in or custom tools to query the database, generate responses using RAG, execute functions, perform web searches, or send notifications using e-email or Slack. All that while maintaining context across multi-turn conversations within the database.

The development process starts with an Agent Team. Each agent team is comprised of one or more agents, that in turn is assigned to one or more tasks. Each task may have access to one or more tools to accomplish its goals.

With this release, you will find additional database objects in the C##CLOUD$SERVICE schema, including the following:

  • Package for creating, dropping, enabling, and disabling Select AI Agent artifacts.
    • DBMS_CLOUD_AI_AGENT
  • Views for...
    • Agent, task, and tool definitions.
      • USER_AI_AGENTS
      • USER_AI_AGENTS_ATTRIBUTES
      • USER_AI_AGENT_TOOL
      • USER_AI_AGENT_TOOL_ATTRIBUTES
      • USER_AI_AGENTS
      • USER_AI_AGENT_TASK_ATTRIBUTES
      • USER_AI_AGENT_TEAMS
      • USER_AI_AGENT_TEAM_ATTRIBUTES
    • History of user interactions, task executions, and tool use that may be helpful for providing traceability.
      • USER_AI_AGENT_TEAM_HISTORY
      • USER_AI_AGENT_TASK_HISTORY
      • USER_AI_AGENT_TOOL_HISTORY

NOTE

Each of the views listed come with their "DBA" counterpart.

Here are some steps that should provide you a quickstart to the agentic AI world in your ADB. Yes, it's already in there.

NOTE

This blog post is published on the same day that I'll be speaking alongside Heli Helskyaho on pretty much the same topic at Oracle AI World 2025 (OAIW25). The code for Select AI Agent is what we will be presenting at our session.

If you're going to be at OAIW25, our session information is as follows:

Session Title: Building Intelligent Apps Using Oracle APEX, Generative AI, and Agentic AI
Session Code: LRN1354
Date and Time: Oct 15, 3.30 PM to 4.15 PM PDT

  1. Create a database credential, if you don't already have one. If you have previously worked with Select AI, then this is probably a simple step. Define the variables as per your environment and tenant.

    begin
      begin
        dbms_cloud.drop_credential(
          credential_name => '&credential_name.'
        );
      exception
        when others then null;
      end;

      dbms_cloud.create_credential(
        credential_name => '&credential_name.'
        , user_ocid => '&user_ocid.'
        , tenancy_ocid => '&tenancy_ocid.'
        , private_key => '&private_key.'
        , fingerprint => '&fingerprint.'
      );
    end;

  2. Create an AI profile for the agent. Here, I am using the OCI Generative AI service, and I will need to define an embedding model, as well as a chat model to be used by the agent. The embedding model I have used is cohere.embed-english-v3.0, and for the chat model, I have experimented with a few, and so far, xai.grok-4-fast-reasoning seems to perform the best, and definitely the fastest.

    begin
      begin
        dbms_cloud_ai.drop_profile(
          profile_name => '&ai_profile_name.'
        );
      exception
        when others then null;
      end;

      dbms_cloud_ai.create_profile(
        profile_name => '&ai_profile_name.',
        attributes => '{
              "provider": "oci",
              "credential_name": "OCI_CRED",
              "model": "&model.",
              "embedding_model": "&embedding_model.",
              "region": "&region.",
              "temperature": 0,
              "max_tokens": 4096
          }'
      );
    end;

  3. Define one or more tools that the agent can use to achieve its goals. Tools can be of types:

    • EMAIL. Sends emails when configured. Uses the dbms_cloud_notification package.
    • SLACK. Uses the dbms_cloud_notification package to send messages to Slack.
    • WEB_SEARCH. Performs a web search using OpenAI’s API. OpenAI credentials are required.
    • RAG. Perform a RAG search using the Select AI Vector index.
    • SQL. Queries the database using Select AI.

    To limit the length of this blog post, I will just provide an example of one tool of type SQL.

    1. If you don't already have one, first create an AI profile for the database objects that Select AI has access to. For example: 
      begin
        begin
          dbms_cloud_ai.drop_profile(
            profile_name => '&ai_profile_name._for_inventory'
          );
        exception
          when others then null;
        end;

        dbms_cloud_ai.create_profile(
          profile_name => '&ai_profile_name._for_inventory',
          attributes => '{
                "provider": "oci",
                "credential_name": "OCI_CRED",
                "object_list": [{"owner": "demo02", "name": "FLEET_PART"}],
                "comments": true,
                "annotations": true
            }'
          , description => 'AI profile for searching the fleet part table'
        );
      end;
    2. Next, define the tool using this AI profile. 
      declare
        c_tool_name constant varchar2(128) := 'inventory_search_tool';
      begin
        begin
          dbms_cloud_ai_agent.drop_tool(
            tool_name => c_tool_name
          );
        exception
          when others then null;
        end;

        dbms_cloud_ai_agent.create_tool(
          tool_name => c_tool_name
          , attributes => json_object(
            'tool_type' value 'SQL'
              , 'tool_params' value json_object(
                'profile_name' value '&ai_profile_name._for_inventory'
              )
          )
          , description => trim(q'[
      This tool is used for searching the fleet part inventory. It should be used to
      lookup fleet parts using either the part number or description.
          ]')
        );
      end;

  4. Define one or more tasks that the agent needs to perform. In my demo, there are two tools. The second is of type RAG that allows the agent to look up PDF copies of different car operating manuals. The RAG tool, again, uses one of Select AI's many features.

    declare
      c_task_name constant varchar2(128) := 'diagnose_car_issue_task';
    begin
      begin
        dbms_cloud_ai_agent.drop_task(c_task_name);
      exception
        when others then null;
      end;

      dbms_cloud_ai_agent.create_task(
        task_name => c_task_name
        , attributes => json_object(
            'instruction' value trim(q'[
    You are a polite, and experienced car mechanic. Follow up on the customer's query:
    {query}

    Keep in mind the following:
    1. If there are insufficient details describing the problem to make a diagnosis.
      then request more information.
    2. With the problem description, search the mechanic's guide (diagnostic_tool)
      for a relevant car owner manual to troubleshoot the problem.
    3. Use the appropriate tool to search the fleet part inventory. Use the part
      number to search for the part first. If not found, try using the description.
      When searching by description, it will be helpful to use the database's
      semantic search capabilities. An example of a query is as follows:
        with desired_part as (
          select vector_embedding(ALL_MINILM_L6_V2 using 'the_search_term' as data)
            as search_vector
        )
        select part_number, description
        from fleet_part p, desired_part d
        order by cosine_distance(p.column_with_vector_embedding, d.search_vector)
        fetch approx first 1 rows only with target accuracy 90
    4. If there are sufficient quantities of the identified fleet part, then suggest
      to the customer to make an appointment to bring the vehicle in for repairs.
            ]')
            , 'tools' value json_array(
                'diagnostic_tool'
                , 'inventory_search_tool'
            )
          )
      );
    end;

  5. Create an agent, assign it the AI profile that defines the LLM that it will send requests to, and provide it a role.

    declare
      c_agent_name constant varchar2(128) := 'mechanic_agent';
    begin
      begin
        dbms_cloud_ai_agent.drop_agent(c_agent_name);
      exception
        when others then null;
      end;

      dbms_cloud_ai_agent.create_agent(
        agent_name => c_agent_name
        , attributes => json_object(
          'profile_name' value '&ai_profile_name.'
          , 'role' value trim(q'[
    You are a friendly and experienced car mechanic that is able to diagnose and
    find solutions to common car problems.
          ]')
          , 'enable_human_tool' value 'True'
        )
      );
    end;

  6. Finally, create an agent team. The team can be made up of one or more agents. Each agent will be assigned .

    declare
      c_agent_team_name constant varchar2(128) := 'mechanic_agent_team';
    begin
      begin
        dbms_cloud_ai_agent.drop_team(c_agent_team_name);
      exception
        when others then null;
      end;

      begin
        dbms_cloud_ai.drop_profile('agent$' || c_agent_team_name);
      exception
        when others then null;
      end;

      dbms_cloud_ai_agent.create_team(
        team_name => c_agent_team_name
        , attributes => json_object(
          'agents' value json_array(
            json_object(
              'name' value 'mechanic_agent'
              , 'task' value 'diagnose_car_issue_task'
            )
          )
          , 'process' value 'sequential'
        )
      );
    end;

Once the agent team is ready, you can "talk" to the Select AI Agent either using:

  • The "select ai {{your_prompt}}" interface; or
  • The dbms_cloud_ai_agent.run_team PL/SQL call.

For the Oracle APEX developers, the second option is what you'd want to use.

To perform these natural language interactions in a tool like SQLcl or the SQL Developer VS code plugin, first, set the agent team:

begin
  dbms_cloud_ai.set_conversation_id(null);
  dbms_cloud_ai_agent.set_team(team_name  => 'mechanic_agent_team');
end;

From there, simply interact with the database using the prefix select ai agent, for example:

select ai agent My car won't start!;

Here's Select AI Agent in action through an Oracle APEX application.

NOTE

This unedited screen capture was done before I updated the application to use Grok 4 Fast, so you might have to watch it at a higher speed. I will update it after the conference. Sorry about that.

Am I Obsolete?​

The advent and proliferation of LLMs, RAG, and AI agents in the last few years, greatly reminds me of the end of the era for film cameras. As they say, AI won't take away your jobs, but the person who uses AI will. The scary bit about AI agents is it's incredible ability to be "trained" and perform some human task at an extremely fast speed.

Then There Are Agentic Workflows​

As I end this #JoelKallmanDay blog post, I just wanted to mention some interesting non-Oracle material that I came across recently. If you haven't yet heard about n8n, then this YouTube video by Network Chuck is worth a watch. I felt that he did an excellent job describing the power of agentic workflows using a "no-code" platform for his hobbyist adventures.

There are two things that I personally avoid though:

  1. Giving a software agent root access.
  2. Ending technical content with a prayer.

And the second point leads me to my closing.

My Tribute to Joel​

In many ways, the prayer that Network Chuck offered to his listeners at the end of the episode reminded me very much of a man I knew who had great faith in God. Joel was a devout Christian but yet he never needed to cite bible verses, or tell you why you should be a believer. Rather, he preached through his actions, and love for everyone that he met.

Joel, it seems particularly poignant that this post will be released on the day that I present a session at Oracle AI World. Thank you for your encouragement over the years that I was privilege to have known you, for pushing me to do more than what I think I can. I miss that, and I miss your opinions when I asked for them. I miss how you'd always put in good words about me to my bosses. And I miss going to these conferences, and just being able to say "hi".

As I wander off on a new journey, I humbly ask for your prayer and intercession. That I will continue to evolve, be better, and make a positive impact on the lives of everyone I meet.

Call to Action​

If any of these interests you at all, or you need further help getting started, please feel free to reach out using the link below. As always, thank you for "listening" to my ramblings till the end.
